records.our_prose: You can tell potatoes are ready by the plants, not a set date. Small new potatoes can be dug gently at the side of a plant from about 7 to 8 weeks after planting, and are best eaten fresh. The main crop is ready when the tops turn yellow and die down, about 3 to 4 months after planting. If you want to store them, leave them in the ground about two weeks after the tops die so the skins toughen, then dig on a dry day with a fork, pushing it in well away from the plant so you do not stab the potatoes. Let them dry off out of the sun, brush off the dirt (do not wash them), and keep them in the dark. Always keep potatoes covered and out of the light, because light turns them green and bitter, and green potatoes are mildly poisonous.

records.our_prose: Potatoes are ready to harvest based on the foliage, not a fixed date. New potatoes, thin-skinned and best used fresh, can be dug carefully at the edge of a hill from about 7 to 8 weeks after planting. The main crop is mature when the tops yellow and die back, roughly 90 to 120 days from planting. For storage potatoes, leave them in the ground about two weeks after the vines die so the skins set and toughen, then dig on a dry day, pushing a fork in well outside the hill so you do not spear tubers. Lift, let them dry briefly out of direct sun, brush off soil (do not wash), and cure in the dark at about 50 to 60°F for two weeks before storing. Keep tubers covered and shaded at every stage, since light greens them and produces bitter, mildly toxic solanine.

records.our_prose: Potatoes grow best in acidic soil, roughly pH 5.0 to 6.0, lower than most garden vegetables. The acidity is deliberate disease management: common scab (Streptomyces scabies) is suppressed in acidic soil and worsens as pH rises above about 5.5, especially in dry soil. Where scab is a recurring problem, hold the pH between about 5.0 and 5.3 and keep the soil evenly moist for the 4 to 9 weeks after planting when tubers are forming. Potatoes tolerate a wider band (down to about 4.8 and up to 6.5), and they will grow at neutral pH, but scab pressure climbs with pH, so do not lime a potato bed. A soil test removes the guesswork before planting.

records.our_prose: In the cold-winter North, grow potatoes once, in spring. Plant the cut seed pieces 2 to 4 weeks before your last frost, when the soil has warmed to about 50°F, usually early to mid April in the middle of the region (a little earlier in the warmest parts, later in the coldest). Skip a fall crop here: it gets cold too soon.

records.our_prose: Potato quality starts in loose, well-drained, acidic soil. Work the bed deep and incorporate compost, breaking up clods so the tubers can expand smoothly; heavy clay rots seed pieces and produces knobby, misshapen tubers and is best improved with organic matter or replaced with a raised bed. Aim for an acidic pH, roughly 5.0 to 6.0, to suppress common scab, and do not lime a potato bed. Avoid fresh manure (which encourages scab) and heavy nitrogen (which grows vines over tubers); use well-finished compost and a balanced fertilizer instead. Plant cut, suberized seed pieces 3 to 5 inches deep, 10 to 12 inches apart in rows 30 to 36 inches apart, once the soil reaches about 50°F, and plan to hill soil over the row as the plants grow.

records.our_prose: Grow potatoes from seed potatoes, which are small whole potatoes or cut pieces, bought as certified disease-free stock (not from the grocery store, and not from packets of seed). Cut bigger ones into chunky pieces about the size of an egg, each with one or two eyes (the little dimples that sprout), and let the cut sides dry and heal for a few days before planting. Plant the pieces cut-side down about 3 to 5 inches deep, 10 to 12 inches apart, in rows about 3 feet apart, once the soil has warmed to about 50°F. There is nothing to start indoors and nothing to harden off.

records.source_context: Potatoes also may be grown in trenches to make the process of hilling easier. Potatoes are most often grown from "seed potatoes," which are small tubers or pieces of tubers that sprout into a new plant. Buying certified disease-free seeds can help prevent problems such as potato late blight.

records.our_prose: For baby new potatoes, dig gently at the side of a plant about 7 to 8 weeks after planting, then cover it back up so the rest keep growing. Eat new potatoes fresh, because their thin skins do not store.

records.source_context: These young potatoes still have thin, delicate skins and are considered a delicacy. New potatoes can be harvested about 7 to 8 weeks after planting. Mature potatoes can take 3 to 4 months before they are ready for harvest. Proper crop rotation, clean garden tools and using disease-resistant cultivars will reduce pests and diseases which ultimately improves crop yields.

records.our_prose: Potatoes want steady, even moisture, especially from the time tubers begin forming (around flowering) through bulking. Aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings. Even moisture is what produces smooth, well-shaped tubers; a dry-then-wet swing causes knobby growth, growth cracks, and hollow heart, and it worsens scab.

records.source_context: If the soil becomes too dry, their growth may be seriously limited. Most vegetable crops require 1 inch of water per week for optimum pro- duction. If your area does not receive this amount of rainfall each week during the growing season, you will need to irrigate your garden using overhead sprinklers, soaker hoses, drip tape or hand watering.
